Last February, a three judge panel on the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Sixth Circuit granted death row inmate Michael Bies's habeas petition, holding that the Double Jeopardy clause bars the state from re-litigiating the issue of Bies' mental retardation. The Ohio Supreme Court has affirmed Bies' death sentence in 1996, despite his mental retardation. The Court agreed with lower courts that this mitigating factor was not outweighed by other aggravating factors. Since then, however, the U.S. Supreme Court has held, in  Atkins v. Virginia , that state may not execute the mentally retarded. Bies filed a habeas petition on these grounds, seeking to get a life sentence, prompting prosecutors to re-open the question of Bies' mental retardation. No dice, the Sixth Circuit panel held last fall , as reopening this issue would violate the Double Jeopardy clause. As the opinion by Judge Clay concluded:

   Under the Double Jeopardy Clause, “when an issue of ultimate fact has once been determined by a valid and final judgment, that issue cannot again be litigated between the same parties in any future lawsuit.”  Ashe , 397 U.S. at 443. This rule establishes an absolute bar to a state seeking to relitigate such an issue of ultimate fact, regardless of the correctness of the original decision. . . . We therefore do not concern ourselveswith the merits of Petitioner’s Atkins claim; the only question before this Court is whether the government, having litigated and lost the issue of Petitioner’s mental retardation, is now attempting to reopen this question. . . . Having examined the record in this case, we determine that Petitioner was found to be mentally retarded, under the clinically accepted definition of mental retardation, by a final judgment of the Supreme Court of Ohio.

**WASHINGTON** — Today, in People Not Politicians v. Onder, the U.S. Supreme Court [granted a stay](https://www.supremecourt.gov/orders/courtorders/091026zr_b07d.pdf) of a district court’s order blocking use of Missouri’s lawful congressional map. The effect of the Supreme Court’s order is to ensure that Missouri voters will vote under the state’s lawful 2022 map this November instead of the gerrymandered map passed by the state legislature in 2025.

Campaign Legal Center, the ACLU of Missouri and the ACLU Voting Rights Project (VRP) filed [amicus](https://campaignlegal.org/document/amicus-brief-opposing-stay) [briefs](https://campaignlegal.org/document/amicus-brief-people-not-politicians-v-onder) in both cases at the U.S. Supreme Court this week.

Onder, explained that the federal district court’s order preventing the use of any map other than the unlawful 2025 map was incorrect because the district court lacked jurisdiction, the order violated federal law, and the order violated the Purcell principle by injecting further chaos into Missouri’s elections less than two months before the general election.

* election administration
The US Supreme Court said Missouri can’t use a Republican-drawn congressional map in the November midterm elections, resolving a complicated legal fight that has caused confusion and uncertainty over what will appear on ballots in the state.
In a decision that came Friday without any noted dissents, the justices granted a request by an anti-gerrymandering group to block a lower court ruling that would have required the state to use new district lines favoring Republicans in the Nov. 3 election.
The five-page, unsigned ruling said it was too close to the election for federal courts to impose a new map. The justices said ballots had already been mailed using the old district lines, and absentee, military and overseas voting had begun.
“At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos,” the high court said. The majority pointed to the so-called Purcell principle, named after a 2006 ruling that has come to stand for the notion that federal judges can’t change a state’s voting rules on the eve of an election.
The Supreme Court order is the final word in a multifaceted legal fight over the state’s maps ahead of a midterm election in which Republicans are trying to maintain control of Congress.
Read more: Trump Flexes Legal Muscle to Expand Power Over US Elections
The high court had already ruled twice against the Republican-backed map, which was used during the state’s primary election in August.
Republicans who control the state legislature drew up the new map outside of the traditional redistricting timeline, where lines are reconsidered every decade based on the US census.

The Application
Application to stay Eighth Circuit and Eastern District of Missouri orders that would have required Missouri to use its 2025 congressional map in the 2026 election, after the Missouri Supreme Court held that the 2025 map does not take effect unless approved by voters in a referendum.
From the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit; U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri · Docket

The Case in Brief

Facts of the case
In 2022, Missouri's legislature drew a map of the state's districts for the U.S. House of Representatives, and in 2025 it passed a new map. On September 3, 2026, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that under state law the 2025 map could not take effect unless voters approved it in a referendum, so the 2022 map had to be used in the 2026 election. A group of voters and candidates then sued in federal court, arguing that the U.S. Constitution requires Missouri to use the 2025 map. The Supreme Court had already paused an earlier federal court order requiring the 2025 map, but on September 21 the federal appeals court for the Eighth Circuit ordered the trial court to issue a permanent order (an injunction) requiring the 2025 map.

The Supreme Court just delivered a blunt rebuke to a federal appeals court that tried to force Missouri to switch congressional maps to the Republican Party's preferred gerrymandered map, despite the nation's top court already ruling against it multiple times.

In an unsigned order issued Friday in *People Not Politicians v. Onder*, the Supreme Court stayed a ruling from the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit that would have required Missouri to use its controversial 2025 congressional map in November's midterm election.

The justices' rebuke against the Eighth Circuit was particularly scathing for a Supreme Court decision.

"Given this Court's two prior orders in this litigation, our conclusion that this was error should come as no surprise," the Supreme Court wrote.

That is about as close as Supreme Court prose gets to: We already told you this.

Screenshot

The dispute centers on Missouri's attempt to replace its 2022 congressional map with a new map enacted by the Republican-controlled legislature in 2025. The new map dramatically redraws the Kansas City-based 5th Congressional District, currently represented by Democratic Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, and could give Republicans control of seven of Missouri's eight congressional seats instead of the current six.

But Missouri voters gathered enough signatures to trigger the state's referendum process. The Missouri Supreme Court ultimately concluded that, under state law, the new map could not take effect unless voters approved it.

On September 3, Missouri's highest court ruled that the 2025 map "is not the law and has never been the law" and therefore could not govern the November election unless voters first approved it.

A federal challenge to the reimposition of the 2022 congressional map pending a referendum on the 2025 re-draw, alleging that the referendum violates the federal constitution’s purported reservation of power to the state legislature, and alleging constitutional concerns with holding the general election under a different map than the primary.

On Sept. 8, 2026, the trial court granted a TRO, restoring the mid-decade map for the coming election. The court rejected the “independent state legislature” argument but validated constitutional concerns with holding the general election under a different map than the primary.

On Sept. 10, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed the trial court’s TRO. For practical purposes, that means the 2022 map will govern the 2026 elections.

(On Sept. 21, 2026, the Eighth Circuit ruled on the merits, purporting to direct the trial court to issue a permanent injunction restoring the mid-decade map; the trial court issued that injunction the same day. On Sept. 25, 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed the trial court’s injunction.) ... State supreme court rejected Secretary of State's finding of insufficiency for referendum signatures, implementing 2022 map for the 2026 elections

you.title: 26A388 People Not Politicians v. Onder (09/25/2026)
you.snippet:
PEOPLE NOT POLITICIANS, ET AL. v. ROBERT ONDER, ET AL. ... PER CURIAM. In 2022, the Missouri Legislature enacted a redistricting map for elections to the U. S. House of Representatives. In 2025, the Missouri Legislature enacted a new map. But under the Missouri Constitution as interpreted by the Supreme Court of Missouri, a new law such as the 2025 map does not take effect unless and until approved by voters in a referendum in the next election—at least where, as here, the number of voter signatures on the petition suffices to trigger a referendum.
Therefore, on September 3, 2026, the Missouri Supreme Court ruled that the 2025 redistricting map “is not the law and has never been the law” in Missouri—and will not take effect unless and until approved by Missouri voters by referendum in the 2026 election.
In two orders in the last few weeks, this Court has denied such relief. In the first, the Missouri Secretary of State asked this Court to stay the September 3 decision of the Missouri Supreme Court that had prohibited use of the 2025 map in the general election.
At this late date, ordering reversion to the 2025 map in the midst of an ongoing election would usher in electoral chaos. Purcell protects against such disorder. The Eighth Circuit panel dealt with Purcell by casting blame on the Missouri Supreme Court for its September 3 decision prohibiting use of the 2025 map.

Under the Missouri Constitution, a newly enacted law like the 2025 map does not become effective until approved by voters in a referendum, provided enough signatures are collected for such a petition. The Missouri Supreme Court held in September 2026 that the 2025 map “is not the law and has never been the law” and would not take effect unless approved in the 2026 election referendum, so the 2022 map remained in force for the upcoming election.
After the Missouri Supreme Court’s ruling, a group of voters and candidates filed suit in federal court, arguing that the U.S. Constitution required Missouri to use the 2025 map in the 2026 election. The U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri issued a temporary restraining order on September 8, effectively requiring the use of the 2025 map.
